newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. says it has put Iraq in a straitjacket.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says it has put Iraq in a straitjacket.

text.p: The United States said on Saturday it had put a "strategic strait-jacket" on Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and was sending enough military force to the Gulf to keep him in check.

President Bill Clinton, who ordered two cruise missile attacks against Iraqi targets last week, said in his weekly radio address: "This action tightened the strategic strait-jacket on Saddam, making it harder for him to threaten Saudi Arabia and Kuwait and easier for us to stop him if he does."

"The United States will take whatever steps are necessary to protect our pilots as they enforce the expanded no-fly zone and to defend our strategic interests," Clinton said. "I have ordered sufficient forces to the region to give us that capability."
Clinton has ordered 5,000 troops to Kuwait, to join 1,200 other U.S. soldiers here since August. Eight F-117A Stealth bombers flew into Kuwait at dusk on Friday.
The Stealth planes, which can evade radar, used laser-guided bombs to hit targets in Baghdad in the 1991 Gulf War when a U.S.-led coalition drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait.
Kuwait, in the eye of the latest Gulf storm, said on Saturday that the region would never be safe with Saddam in power in Baghdad.

The small oil-rich state stressed it was not advocating Saddam's overthrow but would discuss possible "future measures" about Iraq with U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry when he visits Kuwait on Sunday.
"The crisis will never be over until Saddam Hussein goes. This cat and mouse game has to stop," Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah told a news conference.
Clinton has sent his defence secretary to the Middle East to discuss potential military moves. Perry is expected to visit Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Bahrain.
Iraq said on Saturday it hoped its decision to suspend missile attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes enforcing no-fly zones would help defuse the military standoff with Washington.
A spokesman for Iraq's ruling Revolutionary Command Council said on Friday evening that attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes patrolling no-fly zones would stop as of midnight local time (2000 GMT).
But the U.S. military buildup continued despite Iraqi reassurances.

The aircraft carrier Enterprise, with 75 warplanes, arrived at the northern end of the Suez Canal on Saturday and was expected to reach the Gulf on Sunday to join the carrier Carl Vinson. The two ships have F-14 fighters adapted to carry laser-guided bombs.
The United States had already moved long-range B-52 bombers to a British base on the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia, within striking distance of Iraq.

The bombers were used to launch cruise missile strikes against Iraq last week in reprisal for Saddam's military incursion into northern Iraq on August 31 in an alliance with one Kurdish faction against another.
The land, air and sea military buildup reflects Washington's doubts about Iraq's latest pronouncements aimed at defusing two weeks of tension with the United States.
Saddam held talks on Saturday with senior military aides about the deployment of Iraq's surface-to-air missile forces and how to confront any attack.

"The meeting discussed...the improvement of confrontation means in the face of any evil possibility that would be necessitated by the future if Almighty wants that, or Satan pushes the enemy into his vicious abysses," the official Iraqi News Agency INA reported.
In the latest deadly manoeuvring between Baghdad and Washington, Saddam can point to some apparent gains.
The Kurdish region had been out of his control since 1991 and under the protection of Gulf War victors.
Now, Baghdad's influence is returning and the allied Operation Provide Comfort to protect the Kurds from Baghdad appears to be crumbling.

The United States is dismantling its aid and intelligence operations in northern Iraq and preparing to evacuate hundreds of Kurds who worked as programme administrators, drivers, guards, messengers and spies.
Tens of thousands of Kurds have already fled. The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said in Geneva it had confirmed that 30,000 Iraqi Kurds had arrived in Iran.
The medical relief group Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors Without Borders) said in Brussels on Saturday it had launched an emergency operation to help the Kurdish refugees in Iran.
"Except for some tents, nothing is available," the group said. "No shelter, no latrines, no medical materials."
